title: People and Family
description: Name the people in a family and the people in the street — mother, father, the Yemeni word for a child, the word for a friend — and attach 'my' and 'your' to them with the endings Sanaa uses.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — family-tree picture as the here-and-now object; the learner points at relatives and produces أمي، أخوك، بنتش with the correct suffix.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 on the listen-and-tap quiz and a correct 'my / your' suffix on four family words
can_do: Name the members of a family

grammar.title: -i, -ak, -ish: my, your (m), your (f)
grammar.explanation: To say 'my', add -i to the end of the word: بيت becomes بيتي, أخت becomes أختي. 'Your' to a man is -ak: بيتك, أختك. 'Your' to a woman is -ish in Sanaa: بيتش, أختش — the ending that marks highland speech, where Aden says -ik. A few family words change shape first: أب 'father' becomes أبوي 'my father', أبوك, أبوش; أخ 'brother' becomes أخوي, أخوك, أخوش. 'His' is -a (or -uh) and 'her' is -ha: بيته, بيتها.

examples.english: This is my mother and this is my father
Is your brother a student? (to a man)
Is your sister from Sanaa? (to a woman)

culture.title: The family question
culture.note: After the greetings, the next thing a Yemeni asks is about your family — كيف الأهل؟ 'how is the family?' — and the only answer needed is بخير الحمد لله; it is not a request for news. Asking a man about his children, his brothers or his parents is warm and normal. Asking a man about his wife by name is not: say كيف الأهل or كيف البيت and he will include her. Between women every question is fine. Show a photo of your own family and you will make friends faster than with any grammar.

phrases.english: How is the household? (polite way to ask after a man's wife and children)
God bless them (on seeing or hearing about children)

vocabulary.teaching_note: Almost always heard with an ending: أمي 'my mother', أمك, أمش. Children say ماما; adults speaking respectfully say الوالدة. A woman with a son is أم + his name, exactly like أبو for a man.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother in a colourful Sanaa house-dress holding a small child on her hip in a sunlit room.
vocabulary.video_hint: Family vlogs where a mother is introduced or called; أمي in the caption.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The bare word is rare; what you hear is أبوي 'my father', أبوك 'your father', أبوه 'his father'. Respectful الوالد is common too, and a man is addressed as أبو + his eldest son's name.
vocabulary.image_scene: A father in a white thob and Sanaa shawl with a janbiya at his belt, hand on a boy's shoulder.
vocabulary.video_hint: A father shown or spoken about; أبوي / الوالد in narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: With endings it takes an extra و: أخوي 'my brother', أخوك, أخوش. Also the word men use to each other in the street — يا أخي 'brother!' — with no family meaning at all.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young men of similar age with arms over each other's shoulders, grinning.
vocabulary.video_hint: Brothers introduced in a vlog; يا أخي in street speech.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Regular with endings: أختي, أختك, أختش. Ends in the خ–ت cluster, good practice for خ before a consonant. Also يا أختي 'sister!' to any woman politely.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young women in bright shawls laughing together on a rooftop, the city behind them.
vocabulary.video_hint: A sister introduced or addressed; أختي in family content.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ولدي 'my son' is what a father says; the same word means a boy generally. Plural أولاد covers children of both sexes when speaking of a family.
vocabulary.image_scene: A father with a hand on the head of a boy of about ten, both looking at the camera.
vocabulary.video_hint: A parent naming a son; ولدي in family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: بنتي 'my daughter'; the same word is 'girl' in general and بنات is the plural. In Hadramawt you will hear بنيت — same word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother adjusting the shawl of a girl of about ten, both smiling.
vocabulary.video_hint: A parent naming a daughter; بنتي in family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni word for family is أهل — 'my people' — not the bookish عائلة or أسرة. أهلي 'my family', كيف الأهل؟ 'how is the family?'. Also 'the people of' a place: أهل صنعاء.
vocabulary.image_scene: An extended family seated on floor cushions around a large shared tray of food.

example.english: How is the family? — Fine, thank God

vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone asking or talking about their family; أهلي in narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: صاحبي 'my friend' is the everyday word; صديق is understood but more formal. Sanaa also uses ربيع — ربيعي 'my mate' — which you will hear constantly among young men.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends sitting on the steps of a tower house sharing a bag of qat leaves and laughing.
vocabulary.video_hint: Friends introduced on camera; صاحبي / ربيعي in speech.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Yemeni doubles the j: rajjaal, not the MSA rajul. Plural رجال. In Aden the ج becomes g: riggaal. Also a compliment — رجّال 'a real man'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A grown man in a thob, shawl and janbiya standing in a market lane, full figure.

example.english: The man is at the mosque

vocabulary.video_hint: A man pointed out or described; رجال in captions.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Sanaa word for a woman, also 'wife' (مرته 'his wife'). One spelling, three words: mara 'woman', marra 'once', and marra 'very' — the vowel length and doubling tell them apart. Aden says حرمة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman in a black abaya and a patterned Sanaa shawl carrying a shopping bag in a market.
vocabulary.video_hint: A woman referred to; مرة / حرمة in speech.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni word for a child — literally 'one who does not know yet'. Not an insult, though the same word is 'ignorant' in MSA. Plural جهّال: عندي ثلاثة جهّال 'I have three kids'. Aden: gaahil.
vocabulary.image_scene: A boy of about six in a small thob and cap kicking a ball in a stone lane.

example.english: The boy is in the street

vocabulary.video_hint: Children on screen being called جاهل / جهال; family and street content.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The feminine of جاهل — a little girl. The pair shows the feminine ة the learner met in طالب / طالبة. Once she is older she is بنت.
vocabulary.image_scene: A girl of about six in a bright dress with braided hair holding a small kitten.

example.english: The little girl is with her mother

vocabulary.video_hint: A small girl on screen; جاهلة in family content.

sound_spotlight.explanation: A doubled letter is held, not repeated — the tongue stays in place twice as long. Sanaa speech is full of these and they change meaning: mara 'woman' against marra 'very'.
The Sanaa 'your (f.)' ending is produced for the first time here. It is a plain sh — nothing else changes in the word.
The rasping خ runs straight into ت with no vowel between. Practise it as one syllable: ukht, then ukhti.

lesson_sequence.detail: A family photo on a phone screen. One line of English: you will learn who everyone is and how to say 'my' and 'your'.
One family-tree illustration; tap each person to hear the word. Mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter.
The remaining six cards (family, friend, man, woman, boy, girl) with audio; second pass with English.
The word is shown bare; tap 'my', 'your (m)' or 'your (f)' and hear the suffixed form. The -ish ending gets its own explanation card.
All twelve, audio only, four-image grid.
Record أمي، أبوي، أخوك، أختش and compare with the model. Feedback on the doubled j and the sh ending.
Counter rolls up. Nudge: describe a family photo to yourself in Arabic tonight.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Open a family photo on your phone and point at each person saying ذا أبوي، ذي أمي… out loud.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Here-and-now production with a real object.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask a Yemeni acquaintance كيف الأهل؟ today and notice that the reply is a formula, not a report.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Practises the culturally correct family question.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor to describe their family and count how many times you hear جاهل or جهّال.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Trains the ear on the Yemeni word for children in natural speech.

video_needs.scene: Family vlogs where members are introduced or called by name; a mother naming her children; friends introduced as صاحبي.
